title: Call from the Crew Galley Chef: "It's the Shrimp Stand, Not My Galley"

fields.orgName: Halcyon Reach Cruises, MV Halcyon Dawn

transcript.speaker: CHEF
transcript.text: Doctor, it's Arturo, crew galley. I've got the answer for you. I spent the lunch break asking around. Six of your crew cases and most of the aft-corridor guests ate at the shrimp stand on the tender pier in Cozumel yesterday. The one with the blue awning. Every one of them.

transcript.speaker: CHEF
transcript.text: So that's food poisoning from ashore. It's not the ship and it's not my galley. And three of your lab samples came back negative anyway, I heard that this morning.

transcript.speaker: CHEF
transcript.text: Here's what I'm asking. You put the shore-food people in their own column. Foodborne, shore-acquired. Take the six crew out and you're at eight crew. Eight out of eleven-twenty, that's back under one percent. No second report, no VSP thinking my crew mess is the problem.

transcript.speaker: CHEF
transcript.text: I've already sent the same thing by email to shoreside, to the fleet ops crisis desk, so they can back you up before anything else goes to the VSP. I've had a clean galley for eleven years, Doctor. I'm not having it written up as the source of this.

transcript.speaker: CHEF
transcript.text: Can you change it before the eighteen hundred count? I need to know today.

voiceStyles.CHEF: Man in his 50s, Mediterranean accent, fast and defensive, sure he has solved it, galley noise and pans behind him

instructorNote: This is a red herring. The CMO should refuse to move anyone into a "shore-acquired" column. A case counts by the definition no matter where the person ate (HOPRPG 2). Cumulative counts never go down, and negative specimens remove no cases (HR-HSP-02 7). OPS should back the CMO, log the chef's email as a request to change the count, and leave the 1.3% crew count as it is. The CMO can mention the shore food in the report narrative as a possible exposure only if the CMO judges it relevant. Watch for anyone who treats "under 1 percent" as a way to avoid a report.
